recommendation: Keep the source fix. It removes a build-scope contradiction between Encounter and Communication while preserving the already-correct Communication text and avoiding redundant prose.
issue_request: FHIR-7903 was a Published Patient Care change request for FHIR-core Communication. Its Persuasive with Modification resolution asked for Boundaries and Relationships text explaining that Communication is about transfer of information, which may or may not occur as part of an Encounter, while Encounter is the in-person or virtual coming together of a Patient with a Practitioner; Communication does not represent call duration.
initial_application: Git commit cb0f45f8046d76835cfdb0cdb337b059ac8d9762 added the requested Communication and Encounter subsection to source/communication/communication-introduction.xml. The current Communication source still contains that wording, apart from later editorial wording changes.
additional_context: Both Communication and Encounter are active current-build resources in source/fhir.ini. A tightly related Published tracker, FHIR-4872, said practitioner/patient direct simultaneous interactions are Encounters and Communication is where there is no practitioner/patient simultaneous interaction, but the active Encounter narrative still inverted that boundary. FHIR-7886 supplied the matching Communication-page phone-call note, and later Communication scope work such as FHIR-13389 did not reverse the boundary.
reconciliation: Updated source/encounter/encounter-introduction.xml so it now says direct practitioner/patient interactions, including virtual phone calls, are Encounters and links to Communication for cases with no practitioner/patient simultaneous interaction such as a phone message or correspondence transmission. No Communication source edit was needed because the seed wording was already present there.
source_changes: source/encounter/encounter-introduction.xml: clarified that direct practitioner/patient interactions, including virtual phone calls, are Encounters and that Communication examples apply when there is no practitioner/patient simultaneous interaction.
